ai.literal: Another man's wife having desired behaving folly world's virtue wealth with those who have seen is not.
ai.translation: The folly of desiring and pursuing another man's wife is not found among those in the world who have truly understood virtue and wealth.
ai.modern: உலகத்தில் அறத்தையும் பொருளையும் ஆராய்ந்து அறிந்தவர்களிடம், பிறனுடைய மனைவியை விரும்பி நடக்கும் அறியாமை இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet condemns the pursuit of another man's wife as an act of sheer ignorance. The word 'poruḷāḷ' literally means 'she who is the property', emphasizing that the woman belongs to another household. The poet states that such 'pētaimai' (folly) does not exist among those who have truly understood 'aṟam' (virtue) and 'poruḷ' (wealth or true purpose) in this world. True understanding of life's ethical and material goals naturally prevents one from committing this foolish transgression.

ai.literal: Among all those who stood outside virtue, fools than those who stood at another man's gate there are not.
ai.translation: Among all those who stand outside the bounds of virtue, there are no greater fools than those who stand at another man's door.
ai.modern: அறத்தை விட்டு விலகி பாவம் செய்தவர்கள் அனைவரிலும், மற்றொருவனின் வீட்டு வாசலில் சென்று நிற்பவர்களை விடப் பெரிய முட்டாள்கள் யாருமில்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares different types of wrongdoers to highlight the sheer foolishness of coveting another man's wife. The word 'அறன்கடை' refers to standing outside moral boundaries, encompassing all those who commit sins. 'பிறன்கடை' literally means another man's gate, painting a vivid picture of a man lurking outside his neighbor's house with illicit intentions. By stating that there are no greater fools than these men, the text emphasizes that adultery is not just a moral failing, but an act of supreme stupidity.

words.gloss: in the house of the trusting

ai.literal: Than the dead different they are not surely, in the house of those who trusted evil having done those who behave.
ai.translation: Those who behave by doing evil in the house of those who trusted them are surely no different from the dead.
ai.modern: தங்களை நம்பியவரின் வீட்டில் தீமை செய்து நடப்பவர்கள், நிச்சயமாக இறந்தவர்களை விட வேறுபட்டவர்கள் அல்லர்.
ai.explanation: This couplet strongly condemns betraying a friend's trust by violating the sanctity of their home. The word 'தெளிந்தார்' refers to those who have placed clear trust in the offender, while 'இல்' means house, specifically pointing to the household or wife in the context of this chapter. By committing 'தீமை' (evil) in such a trusting home, the betrayer loses all moral standing. The poet declares that such people are 'விளிந்தாரின் வேறல்லர்'—no different from the dead—because a life lived with such deceit is devoid of true vitality or virtue.

ai.literal: of whatever measure they are - even if - what - will become - even millet-measure - he who considers not - another man's - house/wife - entering
ai.translation: What does it matter how great a man is? Entering another man's house without the slightest thought renders his greatness worthless.
ai.modern: ஒருவர் எவ்வளவு பெருமை உடையவராக இருந்தாலும் என்ன பயன்? தினையளவு கூட விளைவுகளை ஆராயாமல் பிறனுடைய மனைவியிடம் செல்வது அந்தப் பெருமையை அழித்துவிடும்.
ai.explanation: The couplet questions the value of any greatness a person might possess if they commit the grave error of desiring another man's wife. The word 'எனைத்துணையர்' (of whatever measure) emphasizes that no amount of wealth, power, or learning can compensate for this moral failure. 'தினைத்துணையும் தேரான்' (not considering even a millet's measure) vividly illustrates the complete lack of forethought and moral judgment. Entering another's house ('பிறனில் புகல்') without the slightest reflection renders all other achievements meaningless.

ai.literal: Easy thinking, house he-who-trespasses will-attain always without-perishing will-stand disgrace.
ai.translation: He who trespasses into another's house thinking it is easy will attain a disgrace that stands forever without fading.
ai.modern: இது எளிது என்று நினைத்து அடுத்தவர் வீட்டிற்குள் எல்லை மீறிச் செல்பவன், எக்காலத்திலும் அழியாமல் நிலைத்து நிற்கும் பழியை அடைவான்.
ai.explanation: The couplet warns against the temptation of illicit affairs by highlighting the permanent damage to one's reputation. The word 'il' has multiple meanings including 'not', but here it means 'house', specifically referring to trespassing into a neighbor's home. A person might think such a transgression is easy to commit and hide. However, the resulting disgrace will never perish and will stand against him forever.

ai.literal: Enmity, sin, fear, disgrace, thus all four, depart-not indeed, house transgressor with.
ai.translation: Enmity, sin, fear, and disgrace—these four will never depart from the man who transgresses into another's home.
ai.modern: பகை, பாவம், அச்சம், பழி ஆகிய இந்த நான்கு தீமைகளும் பிறன் மனைவியிடம் வரம்பு மீறிச் செல்பவனை விட்டு ஒருபோதும் நீங்காது.
ai.explanation: This couplet outlines the inevitable consequences of coveting another man's wife, symbolized by crossing the threshold of his house ('இல் இறப்பான்'). The poet lists four distinct burdens: enmity from the aggrieved family, moral sin, constant fear of discovery, and public disgrace. The phrase 'இகவாவாம்' emphasizes that these four destructive forces will permanently attach themselves to the transgressor and never leave him.

ai.literal: Virtue by nature householder he who is called another man she who belongs to womanhood he who does not desire.
ai.translation: He who is called a true householder living by virtue is the one who does not desire the womanhood of her who belongs to another.
ai.modern: அறத்தின் இயல்போடு இல்வாழ்க்கை வாழ்பவன் என்று சொல்லப்படுபவன், மற்றொருவனின் உரிமைக்கு உட்பட்டவளின் பெண்மையை விரும்பாதவனே ஆவான்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the true nature of a virtuous householder. It states that merely living in a household does not make one a true householder; true domestic virtue requires strict moral discipline. The key word 'நயவாதவன்' is formed by joining 'நயவாது' (without desiring) and 'அவன்' (he), emphasizing the complete absence of desire for another man's wife. Thus, the foundation of a righteous family life is built on respecting the boundaries of others.

ai.literal: Another's wife not looking at great manliness, to the noble ones virtue not only excellent conduct.
ai.translation: The great manliness that does not look at another's wife is, to the noble, not just a virtue but the most excellent conduct.
ai.modern: பிறருடைய மனைவியை ஆசையுடன் நோக்காத பெரிய ஆண்மையே, சான்றோர்களுக்கு அறம் மட்டுமன்றி சிறந்த ஒழுக்கமும் ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines true manliness not as physical strength, but as the moral discipline to refrain from coveting another man's wife. The phrase 'pērāṇmai' (great manliness) highlights the immense self-control required for this restraint. For the noble ones, such behavior is not merely a basic virtue ('aṟaṉ') but stands as the highest standard of excellent conduct ('āṉṟa oḻukku'). The poet elevates this specific restraint to the pinnacle of ethical living.

ai.literal: To goodness entitled who if asked, fearful water in the world, to others she who belongs shoulder those who do not touch.
ai.translation: If asked who in this sea-girt world is entitled to true goodness, it is those who do not embrace the shoulders of another man's wife.
ai.modern: அச்சம் தரும் கடலால் சூழப்பட்ட இவ்வுலகில் நன்மைகளுக்கு உரியவர்கள் யார் என்றால், பிறருக்கு உரியவளின் தோள்களைத் தழுவாதவர்களே ஆவர்.
ai.explanation: The couplet asks a rhetorical question about who truly deserves goodness and virtue in this vast world. The answer is those who strictly refrain from touching the shoulders of a woman who belongs to another. The phrase 'fearful water' (நாமநீர்) refers to the awe-inspiring ocean that surrounds the earth, emphasizing the vastness of the world in contrast to the strict, intimate moral boundary of not desiring another's wife.

ai.literal: Virtue he does not limit himself to, evil things even if he does, another man's bound woman's womanhood not desiring is good.
ai.translation: Even if a man does not confine himself to virtue and commits evil deeds, it is still good if he does not desire the womanhood of another man's wife.
ai.modern: ஒருவன் அறத்தின் வரம்பிற்குள் நிற்காமல் பாவச் செயல்களைச் செய்தாலும், அவன் மற்றொருவனுடைய மனைவியின் பெண்மையை விரும்பாமல் இருப்பது அவனுக்கு நல்லதாகும்.
ai.explanation: The couplet contrasts general immorality with the specific sin of desiring another man's wife. The word 'varaiyāṉ' (he who does not limit himself) describes a man who steps outside the boundaries of virtue to commit evil deeds ('alla'). However, the text states that even for such a person, there is goodness ('naṉṟu') if he refrains from desiring ('nayavāmai') the womanhood ('peṇmai') of a woman bound to another man ('piṟaṉ varaiyāḷ'). This emphasizes that respecting the marital boundaries of others is a fundamental good, even when other virtues are absent.
